newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila drafting protest over China Spratly move.
newsitem.headline: Manila drafting protest over China Spratly move.

text.p: Philippine marines steamed towards the disputed Spratly Islands in the South China Sea on Wednesday as Manila voiced strong concern over an alleged incursion by three Chinese warships into an area it claims.

Senior defence department officials insisted the Philippines was simply rotating troops already stationed in the tiny islands and the dispatch of more than 200 marines did not mean it was bolstering its forces in the area.
The Spratlys are a cluster of 190 potentially oil-rich but barren isles, reefs and shoals claimed wholly or in part by China, the Philippines, Vietnam, Taiwan, Malaysia and Brunei.
Manila said on Tuesday it would file a diplomatic protest with Beijing over the latest incident to ruffle relations between the two countries.
"We are drafting a diplomatic note today...calling their attention to the sighting of the Chinese vessels and informing them this has caused concern," a Filipino diplomat told Reuters.

"The note will also remind them that we have a code of conduct which requires that neither side should take any move in the area without first notifying the other," he said, asking not to be identified.

A senior military source said the three Chinese vessels, accompanied by what looked like four fishing boats, were still in the area after a military reconnaissance plane first sighted them last Friday.
One of the frigates has cast anchor while another remained stationary in "a lying-in position", said the source.
"They looked like fishing boats but we can't say if the people on board were really fishermen. We were not able to come any closer," said the officer, who also asked not to be identified.
A government statement said reconnaissance aircraft also discovered a new hut-like structure built over a reef six miles northeast of Kota island, one of the islands which Manila claims.
The sighting of the frigates prompted a special meeting of the cabinet on Monday where the decision to file a protest was made, presidential executive secretary Ruben Torres told reporters.

"We don't know why they are there so let's wait for the Chinese explanation," Torres said. "If they can prove innocent passage then that's all right. If they are there to put up new structures, that's a problem."
Chinese embassy officials were not immediately available for comment but the Manila newspaper Malaya quoted an embassy spokesman as saying the reported incursions "are pure fabrication".

Tension flared between the Philippines and China in 1995 when Manila accused the Chinese of building what it said looked like naval support structures on Mischief Reef. Beijing said they were shelters for fishermen and has refused to dismantle them.
The Philippines has agreed on a code of conduct separately with China and Vietnam under which they agree to exercise self-restraint and not use force in resolving the Spratlys row.
Torres said filing a diplomatic protest "is the strongest action" the Philippines could take for now.
"We expect China's response to such a protest. We are also looking at the structures that were apparently recently built in some islets there," he added.
